author: Meir Y Soloveichik
title: This Is Not Fauda, This Is Real Life - Commentary Magazine
text:
In the 19th century, the German-Jewish artist Moritz Daniel Oppenheim created a painting titled Die Jahrzeit, a scene of a Jew preparing to recite the Kaddish on the date of his parent’s passing. The scene was not set in the synagogue or at the cemetery. Rather, we see a minyan, a Jewish prayer quorum, that has come together in Alsace-Lorraine during the Franco-Prussian war of 1870. These are Jewish soldiers who have fought for Prussia; the Jew reciting the mourner’s prayer is wearing a pickelhaube, the spiked helmet of the German military. The Germanness was, in part, the point: Oppenheim sought to reflect the patriotism of the Jewish soldiers, their willingness to fight and die for the Vaterland. The painting was created with the hope that it would encourage the embrace of Jews in German society. There is, with the hindsight of history, a very painful irony attending the artwork today.
At the same time, Oppenheim was making a powerful point: that the Jews of Prussia would continue to mourn and remember their predecessors, as Jews. The pickelhaube, which the soldier has no doubt been wearing throughout his time at the front, creates a noted contrast with the tallit, the prayer shawl, he has donned to pray in accordance with the traditions of the past. And the fact that his fellow Jews—all soldiers like him—have committed to coming together to form the minyan in order to facilitate this act of faith transforms the scene into one of Jewish faithfulness, loyalty, and love.
By setting this scene in a war zone, Oppenheim also allows us to remember that the Kaddish—a faithful declaration and prayer for the further sanctification of God’s name—reflects not only the memory of those who have passed but faith in the face of mortality itself. As the soldiers gather in an abandoned French home, the man leading the service faces an empty picture frame because the family that fled has taken the painting that it housed. The glass of the frame has a bullet hole in it; as he recites the prayer, the soldier is, visually, staring death in the face. His fellow Jewish soldiers also reflect the experience that war has wrought. One of them is a medic who seems to be meditating on the wounds and deaths he has seen; another cannot stand for the prayer because he is too injured to do so. As they pray together, allowing one of them to remember the passing of his parent, they are also pondering a possible state of affairs in which they no longer live. Throughout all this, their faith remains: The recital of Kaddish continues.
I thought of this painting when I watched the final scene of the recent season of Fauda, the Israeli series about an anti-terror commando squad, which places the horror of October 7 at the center of its storyline. In the conclusion of the final episode, as comrades gather at a cemetery to bid farewell to one of their own, the character of Doron, played by Lior Raz, recites Kaddish at the grave. A cameo occurs just before; it is the appearance of the actor Idan Amedi, whose character (Sagi) arrives to take part in the memorial. Sagi was a central figure in previous seasons of Fauda but was largely absent from this one—because Idan Amedi suffered a terrible injury while at war. Not scripted, not on screen, but in actuality, in Gaza.
Following October 7, Amedi joined his unit and, in uniform, spoke in a short recorded clip of how important it was, to him, to defend his country and its families. “Zeh lo setzinah mi-Fauda,” he said—“this is not a scene from Fauda.” No, he said, “zeh hayyim amitim”—“this is real life.” Soon after, he was horrifically burned in an explosion and devoted months to recovery. Another image of Amedi shows him in the hospital, his face profoundly scarred but showing a good-natured expression, sticking out his tongue. It is the visage of a man who has faced war, mortality, and death, and, who, rather than feeling sorry for himself, feels fortunate to be alive.
Amedi is also a musician, and returning to the stage in 2025, he recognized in the audience a medic who had saved his life. He called the medic up to the stage, and the two soldiers embraced. In 2026, Amedi returned not to a troupe but to a troop; he did not take part in the filming of much of the fifth season of Fauda, but he did go back to his unit. While on duty, he took part in rescuing the body of Ran Gvili, a courageous combat officer who fell on October 7, and Amedi later sang at Gvili’s funeral.
In a moment in that episode of Fauda, art and actuality converged. We know that this actor, who suddenly appears when the Kaddish commences, has himself only recently been at war, a war in which a member of Fauda’s production team, Matan Meir, was killed in action. We know as well that he has certainly attended the funerals of fallen comrades and has taken part in the quorums in which Kaddish has been recited. He has done all this as a soldier, and not in a Prussia where Jews must beg for inclusion but in the miraculous resurrected Jewish state. And as Kaddish is recited on screen, we realize: This too is hayyim amitim, true life. This is how Jews have always lived in the face of death, and this is how Jews will continue to live. Kaddish will continue to be said; Jews will continue to gather to say it; and in the process, they will reflect the faith, loyalty, and love of centuries past.
In a world in which we must suffer the fatuous fulminations of Mark Ruffalo and Hannah Einbinder, this actor’s cameo carried a profundity that defied its brevity. And in a season of the Jewish calendar in which we ask for life, Amedi reminds us of what a blessing it is to be alive, and to live a Jewish life today.
